subject: math
title: Grade 6 Budgeting and Consumer Math: Budgets, Needs and Wants, Unit Prices and Discounts
seo_title: Grade 6 Budgeting and Consumer Math Worksheets: Unit Price, Discounts and Saving Goals (Free, Answer Key, BC Curriculum)
standard_text: Financial literacy – simple budgeting and consumer math
meta_desc: Free Grade 6 math worksheets on budgeting and consumer math for the BC curriculum: income and expenses, needs and wants, unit prices and the best buy, discounts and sale prices, and saving goals. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Compare unit prices, not total prices: the lowest price per 100 g, per litre or per item is the best buy.
key_sub: A budget is balanced when income equals expenses plus savings. Pay for needs first. For a discount, find the percent of the regular price and subtract it.
body_html:
Budgets: income and expenses

A budget is a plan for your money. Income is money coming in. Expenses are money going out. Savings are part of the plan too. A budget is balanced when income = expenses + savings.

Needs and wants

A need is something you must have to be safe and healthy: food, water, a home, warm clothes. A want is nice to have, but you can live without it. Plan for needs first.

Unit prices and the best buy

A unit price is the price for one unit, such as per 100 g, per litre or per item. To find the best buy, compare unit prices, not total prices.

Discounts

A discount takes money off the regular price. Find the percent of the regular price and subtract it. Or find the percent you still pay: 25% off means you pay 75%.

Example

A $60 rain jacket is 25% off. What is the sale price?

Discount: 25% of $60 = $60 ÷ 4 = $15. Sale price: $60 − $15 = $45. Or: 75% of $60 = $45.

Answer: $45

Saving goals

Subtract what you already have from the goal. Divide what is left by the amount you save each week. If the answer is not a whole number, round up.

Example

You want a $90 video game. You have $18 and save $8 a week. How many weeks will it take?

Still needed: $90 − $18 = $72. $72 ÷ $8 = 9. It takes 9 weeks.

Answer: 9 weeks

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Picking the package with the lowest total priceCompare the price per 100 g, per litre or per item
Forgetting that savings are part of the planIncome = expenses + savings
25% off $60 = $60 − 25 = $35Find 25% of $60 ($15), then subtract: $45
$90 ÷ $12 = 7.5, so 7 weeksRound up: after 7 weeks you are still short, so 8 weeks
Forgetting money you already savedSubtract it from the goal first

faq.q: What is budgeting and consumer math in Grade 6 BC math?
faq.a: It is the Grade 6 financial literacy topic in the BC curriculum. Students plan simple budgets with income and expenses, sort needs and wants, compare unit prices to find the best buy, and work out discounts and saving goals.

faq.q: How do you find the best buy using unit price?
faq.a: Divide each price by its amount to get the price per 100 g, per litre or per item, then pick the lowest. For example, $5.20 for 400 g is $1.30 per 100 g and $8.25 for 750 g is $1.10 per 100 g, so the bigger box is the better buy.

faq.q: How do I explain needs and wants to my child?
faq.a: A need is something you must have to be safe and healthy, like food, a home and a warm coat; a want is nice to have, like a video game. A good budget pays for needs first, then savings and wants.

faq.q: How do you make a simple budget for kids?
faq.a: List the money coming in (allowance, chores, gifts), then the money going out and the amount to save. If income equals expenses plus savings, the budget is balanced.

items.q: In a budget, what is income?
c: Money you earn or are given
items.e: Income is money coming in: an allowance, pay for a job, or a gift of money. Money going out is an expense.

items.q: Which one is an expense?
items.e: An expense is money going out. Buying a soccer ball is an expense. The others are income: money coming in.

items.q: Wei gets a $20 allowance and earns $15 walking a neighbour’s dog each week. What is his total income each week?
items.e: Add all the money coming in: $20 + $15 = $35. ($5 subtracts instead of adding; $20 counts only the allowance.)

items.q: This week Noah spends $12 on a movie, $6.50 on snacks and $8 on bus fare. What are his total expenses?
items.e: Add the money going out, lining up the decimal points: $12.00 + $6.50 + $8.00 = $26.50. ($26 drops the 50¢; $20.50 forgets the bus fare; $14.50 forgets the movie.)

items.q: When is a budget balanced?
c: When income equals expenses plus savings
When you spend all your money on wants
When expenses are more than income
items.e: A budget is balanced when every dollar of income is planned for: expenses + savings = income.

items.q: Liam earns $15 a week. How much does he earn in 4 weeks?
items.e: 4 × $15 = $60. ($19 adds 4 instead of multiplying; $45 is 3 weeks and $75 is 5 weeks.)

items.q: Savings are part of the plan. How much money is not planned for yet?
items.e: Income: $40 + $36 = $76. Planned: $15 + $12 + $10 + $25 = $62. $76 − $62 = $14. ($39 forgets to count the savings; $62 is the planned money, not what is left; $138 adds income and planned money.)

items.q: Arjun earns $14 an hour babysitting. On Saturday he babysits for 3.5 hours. How much does he earn?
items.e: $14 × 3.5: $14 × 3 = $42 and $14 × 0.5 = $7. $42 + $7 = $49. ($42 leaves out the half hour; $56 uses 4 hours; $17.50 adds instead of multiplying.)

items.q: Hana’s income is $60 this month. Her expenses are $72. What does this mean?
c: She spends $132 more than she has
She spends $12 more than she has
items.e: Expenses are more than income: $72 − $60 = $12. She is $12 short and must cut $12 of expenses or earn more.

items.q: Sofia wants this budget to be balanced. How much should go to savings?
items.e: Income: $25 + $45 = $70. Expenses: $32 + $9 = $41. Savings: $70 − $41 = $29. ($38 forgets the snacks; $61 forgets the cleats; $111 adds everything together.)

items.q: A music app costs $8 a month. How much does it cost for one year?
items.e: A year has 12 months. 12 × $8 = $96. ($80 uses 10 months; $104 uses 13 months; $416 uses 52, the number of weeks.)

items.q: Ryan’s income is $60 a month and his expenses are $45 a month. He saves the rest. How much does he save in 6 months?
items.e: Savings each month: $60 − $45 = $15. In 6 months: 6 × $15 = $90. ($360 is all the income; $270 is all the expenses; $15 is only one month.)

items.q: A bus ride costs $2.45. Lucas takes 8 rides. How much does he spend?
items.e: 8 × $2.45 = 8 × $2 + 8 × $0.45 = $16 + $3.60 = $19.60. ($16.45 multiplies only the dollars; $196.00 and $1.96 put the decimal point in the wrong place.)

items.q: This budget plans $10 more than the income. Which change balances it?
items.e: Planned: $30 + $15 + $15 = $60, but income is $50. To balance, plan $10 less: spend $10 less on snacks (now $5). Saving more or earning less makes the gap bigger.

items.q: Leah earns $150 at a summer job and spends 40% of it. How much is left?
items.e: If 40% is spent, 60% is left. 10% of $150 is $15, so 60% is 6 × $15 = $90. ($60 is the 40% spent; $110 subtracts 40 dollars, not 40%; $210 adds 40% instead of taking it away.)

items.q: Job A pays $12 an hour for 5 hours. Job B pays $70 for the same afternoon. Which pays more?
items.e: Job A: 5 × $12 = $60. Job B: $70. $70 − $60 = $10, so Job B pays $10 more. ($58 compares $70 with $12, the pay for one hour.)

items.q: Mei’s monthly income is $120. She plans to save 20% of it. How much will she save each month?
items.e: 10% of $120 is $12, so 20% is 2 × $12 = $24. ($20 uses the percent as dollars; $6 divides by 20; $96 is the 80% left to spend.)

items.q: What percent of Harjot’s income goes to savings?
items.e: Income: $45 + $15 = $60. Savings: $15. $15 out of $60 = 1/4 = 25%. (15% uses the dollars as the percent; 33% compares savings with expenses, $15 out of $45; 75% is the rest.)

items.q: Ava earns $20 a week and spends $12.50 a week. She saves the rest. How much has she saved after 4 weeks?
items.e: Saved each week: $20.00 − $12.50 = $7.50. After 4 weeks: 4 × $7.50 = $30. ($80 is all the income; $50 is what she spends; $7.50 is only one week.)

items.q: In April Zara earns $18 for each of 3 car washes and $25 for each of 2 yard clean-ups. She spends $80 on new runners. How much is left?
items.e: Income: 3 × $18 + 2 × $25 = $54 + $50 = $104. Left: $104 − $80 = $24. ($104 forgets the runners; $31 mixes up the counts, 3 × $25 + 2 × $18; $184 adds the $80.)

items.q: What is a need?
c: Something nice that you can live without
Something you must have to live safely and be healthy
items.e: A need is something you must have to be safe and healthy, like food, water, a home and warm clothes. A want is nice to have, but you can live without it.

items.q: Which one is a need?
items.e: You must eat to stay healthy, so healthy food for meals is a need. The others are wants.

items.q: Which one is a want?
c: A phone case with a cool design
items.e: You can live without a fancy phone case, so it is a want. Water, warm clothes and a home are needs.

items.q: It rains a lot in Vancouver in the fall. A student walks to school every day. Which one is a need?
items.e: Staying dry and warm keeps you healthy, so a rain jacket that fits is a need. The others are wants.

items.q: Which one is a need for a family?
c: Heat and electricity for the home
items.e: A home must be warm and safe, so heat and electricity are needs. The others are wants.

items.q: Why can shoes be a need or a want?
c: Shoes are never in a budget
Shoes are a need only if they are expensive
One pair that fits is a need; an extra fancy pair is a want
items.e: You need shoes that fit to walk safely. A second, fancy pair is nice but not needed, so it is a want.

items.q: In a grocery cart there is milk, bread, apples and a chocolate bar. Which one is a want?
items.e: Milk, bread and apples are healthy foods for meals: needs. The chocolate bar is a treat: a want.

items.q: Money is tight this month. What is the best order to plan spending?
c: Needs first, then wants if money is left
Whatever you see first in the store
items.e: Pay for needs first so you are safe and healthy. Use any money left over for savings and wants.

items.q: A family’s list: groceries $85, winter boots $60, a video game $70 and a movie night $25. How much is for needs?
items.e: Needs: groceries and winter boots. $85 + $60 = $145. ($95 is the wants; $240 is everything; $215 counts the video game as a need.)

items.q: How much more is planned for needs than for wants?
items.e: Needs: $24 + $38 = $62. Wants: $29 + $16 = $45. $62 − $45 = $17. ($107 adds the two totals; $45 is only the wants; $9 compares only gym shoes and skateboard wheels.)

items.q: Olivia has $50. She needs $32 for a bus pass and lunches this week. How much is left for wants and savings?
items.e: Pay the needs first: $50 − $32 = $18 left. ($32 is the needs; $82 adds instead of subtracting; $22 takes 0 − 2 as 2 instead of regrouping.)

items.q: Simran has $20. She can buy a book or go to a movie, but not both. She buys the book. What does she give up?
c: Both the book and the movie
items.e: When you choose one thing, you give up the other. This is a trade-off. Buying the book means she gives up the movie.

items.q: A family’s weekly budget is $400. They spend $240 on needs. What percent of the budget is needs?
items.e: $240 out of $400 = 240/400 = 60/100 = 60%. (40% is the rest; 24% comes from the dollars, 240; 167% divides the wrong way, 400 ÷ 240.)

items.q: Kai has $40 for wants. Which two things can he buy without going over $40?
items.e: Book + puzzle = $14.50 + $22.75 = $37.25, which is under $40. The other pairs cost $42.50, $50.75 and $47.99.

items.q: After paying for needs, a family has $150 left. They want a $90 bike and a $70 tablet case. Can they buy both?
items.e: $90 + $70 = $160, which is more than $150. $160 − $150 = $10, so they are $10 short. (“$60 left” counts only the bike.)

items.q: Jasleen’s family has $80 for the week. 55% goes to needs. How much is left for wants and savings?
items.e: If 55% is needs, 100% − 55% = 45% is left. 10% of $80 is $8, so 40% is $32 and 5% is $4. 45% = $36. ($44 is the needs; $45 uses the percent as dollars; $25 subtracts 55 from 80.)

items.q: Chloe gets $60 for her birthday. She puts 50% into savings and spends $18 on school supplies (a need). She spends the rest on a want. How much is that?
items.e: Savings: 50% of $60 = $30. Left: $60 − $30 − $18 = $12. ($30 is the savings; $42 forgets the savings; $48 forgets the school supplies.)

items.q: A family earns $3200 a month. They spend $2400 on needs such as rent, food and heat. What percent is that?
items.e: 2400/3200 = 24/32 = 3/4 = 75%. (25% is the part left; 24% comes from the dollars, 2400; 133% divides the wrong way: 3200 ÷ 2400.)

items.q: Wei has $70. He needs 4 lunches at $12 each for a school camp. He wants a $25 hoodie. After the lunches, how much more money does he need for the hoodie?
items.e: Lunches (needs): 4 × $12 = $48. Left: $70 − $48 = $22. The hoodie costs $25, so he needs $25 − $22 = $3 more. ($22 is the money left; $45 subtracts only the hoodie; $13 takes away only one lunch.)

items.q: Noah is saving for new hockey skates because his old skates are too small and he plays on a team. He also wants a new video game. Which should he buy first?
c: Both, even if there is not enough money
items.e: Skates that fit are needed to play safely on the team, so they come first. The skates are the need here; the game is a want.

items.q: A shelf tag says “$0.60 per 100 g”. What does this unit price tell you?
c: How many grams are in the package
The cost of the whole package
The cost of 100 g of the food
items.e: A unit price is the price for one unit of an item, here 100 g. It lets you compare packages of different sizes fairly.

items.q: A 500 g bag of pasta costs $2.50. What is the price per 100 g?
items.e: There are 5 groups of 100 g in 500 g, so divide: $2.50 ÷ 5 = $0.50 per 100 g. Check: $0.50 × 5 = $2.50. (Multiplying instead of dividing gives $12.50.)

items.q: A 2 L carton of milk costs $4.30. What is the price per litre?
items.e: There are 2 groups of 1 L in 2 L, so divide: $4.30 ÷ 2 = $2.15 per litre. Check: $2.15 × 2 = $4.30. (Multiplying instead of dividing gives $8.60.)

items.q: A carton of 12 eggs costs $5.40. What is the price per egg?
items.e: There are 12 groups of 1 egg in 12 eggs, so divide: $5.40 ÷ 12 = $0.45 per egg. Check: $0.45 × 12 = $5.40. (Multiplying instead of dividing gives $64.80.)

items.q: A 400 g box of BC blueberries costs $5.20. What is the price per 100 g?
items.e: There are 4 groups of 100 g in 400 g, so divide: $5.20 ÷ 4 = $1.30 per 100 g. Check: $1.30 × 4 = $5.20. (Multiplying instead of dividing gives $20.80.)

items.q: A 2 kg bag of Okanagan apples costs $6.40. What is the price per 100 g?
items.e: There are 20 groups of 100 g in 2 kg (2000 g), so divide: $6.40 ÷ 20 = $0.32 per 100 g. Check: $0.32 × 20 = $6.40. Remember 1 kg = 1000 g. ($3.20 is the price per kilogram, not per 100 g.) (Multiplying instead of dividing gives $128.00.)

items.q: Two boxes of crackers are different sizes. What should you compare to find the better buy?
c: The price for the same amount, such as per 100 g
items.e: A bigger box usually costs more in total, so totals do not tell you which is cheaper. Compare the price for the same amount: the unit price.

items.q: Which box of cereal is the better buy?
c: Both cost the same per 100 g
items.e: Compare the price per 100 g, not the total price. Box A: $5.20 ÷ 4 = $1.30 per 100 g; Box B: $8.25 ÷ 7.5 = $1.10 per 100 g. Box B has the lower price per 100 g, so it is the better buy. (Box A has the lowest total, but you get less.)

items.q: Which box of crackers is the better buy?
c: Both cost the same per 100 g
items.e: Compare the price per 100 g, not the total price. Box A: $2.40 ÷ 2 = $1.20 per 100 g; Box B: $3.90 ÷ 3 = $1.30 per 100 g. Box A has the lower price per 100 g, so it is the better buy. A bigger box is not always the better buy.

items.q: Which jug of apple juice is the better buy?
c: Both cost the same per litre
items.e: Compare the price per litre, not the total price. Jug A: $2.60 ÷ 1 = $2.60 per litre; Jug B: $4.80 ÷ 2 = $2.40 per litre. Jug B has the lower price per litre, so it is the better buy. (Jug A has the lowest total, but you get less.)

items.q: A 500 g jar of peanut butter costs $3.50. A 1 kg jar costs $6.00. Liam says the 500 g jar is the better buy because it costs less. Is he right?
c: No, the 1 kg jar costs less per 100 g
No, the two jars cost the same per 100 g
Yes, it costs less in total
Yes, small jars always cost less per 100 g
items.e: Compare unit prices, not totals. 500 g jar: $3.50 ÷ 5 = $0.70 per 100 g. 1 kg jar: $6.00 ÷ 10 = $0.60 per 100 g. The 1 kg jar costs less per 100 g, so it is the better buy (if you will use it all).

items.q: A box of 6 granola bars costs $3.30. A box of 10 granola bars costs $5.00. Which is the better buy?
c: Both cost the same per bar
items.e: Compare the price per bar, not the total price. The box of 6: $3.30 ÷ 6 = $0.55 per bar; The box of 10: $5.00 ÷ 10 = $0.50 per bar. The box of 10 has the lower price per bar, so it is the better buy. (The box of 6 has the lowest total, but you get less.)

items.q: A 1.5 kg bag of carrots costs $3.45. What is the price per kilogram?
items.e: 1.5 kg = 1.5 × 1 kg, so divide: $3.45 ÷ 1.5 = $2.30 per kilogram. Check: $2.30 × 1.5 = $3.45. (Multiplying instead of dividing gives $5.18.)

items.q: A 250 g pack of smoked salmon costs $9.50. What is the price per 100 g?
items.e: 250 g = 2.5 × 100 g, so divide: $9.50 ÷ 2.5 = $3.80 per 100 g. Check: $3.80 × 2.5 = $9.50. (Multiplying instead of dividing gives $23.75.)

items.q: An 800 g bag of cherries costs $6.40. What is the price per kilogram?
items.e: 800 g = 0.8 × 1 kg, so divide: $6.40 ÷ 0.8 = $8.00 per kilogram. Check: $8.00 × 0.8 = $6.40. 800 g is less than 1 kg, so 1 kg costs more than $6.40. (Multiplying instead of dividing gives $5.12.)

items.q: Which bag of rice is the best buy?
c: They all cost the same per kilogram
items.e: Compare the price per kilogram, not the total price. Bag A: $3.20 ÷ 1 = $3.20 per kilogram; Bag B: $6.00 ÷ 2 = $3.00 per kilogram; Bag C: $16.00 ÷ 5 = $3.20 per kilogram. Bag B has the lowest price per kilogram, so it is the best buy. (Bag A has the lowest total, but you get less.)

items.q: A 650 g tub of yogurt costs $3.90. A pack of 4 yogurt cups, 100 g each, costs $2.80. Which is the better buy?
c: Both cost the same per 100 g
items.e: Compare the price per 100 g, not the total price. The tub: $3.90 ÷ 6.5 = $0.60 per 100 g; The 4 cups: $2.80 ÷ 4 = $0.70 per 100 g. The tub has the lower price per 100 g, so it is the better buy. (The 4 cups has the lowest total, but you get less.)

items.q: Grapes cost $4.40 per kilogram. How much do 2.5 kg cost?
items.e: Multiply the unit price by the amount: $4.40 × 2.5 = $8.80 + $2.20 = $11.00. ($8.80 is only 2 kg; $6.90 adds 4.40 + 2.5; $1.76 divides.)

items.q: One notebook costs $1.75. A pack of 5 notebooks costs $7.50. How much do you save on each notebook by buying the pack?
items.e: Pack price per notebook: $7.50 ÷ 5 = $1.50. Saving on each: $1.75 − $1.50 = $0.25 (25¢). ($1.25 is the saving on all 5; $1.50 is the pack’s unit price.)

items.q: A 400 mL bottle of shampoo costs $5.60. A 1 L bottle costs $12.00. Which is the better buy?
c: You cannot compare mL and L
Both cost the same per 100 mL
items.e: Compare the price per 100 mL, not the total price. The 400 mL bottle: $5.60 ÷ 4 = $1.40 per 100 mL; The 1 L bottle: $12.00 ÷ 10 = $1.20 per 100 mL. The 1 L bottle has the lower price per 100 mL, so it is the better buy. (The 400 mL bottle has the lowest total, but you get less.)

items.q: A $40 hoodie is 10% off. How much is the discount?
items.e: 10% is one tenth. $40 ÷ 10 = $4 off. ($36 is the sale price, not the discount; $30 subtracts 10 dollars; $0.40 is 1%.)

items.q: A $40 hoodie is 10% off. What is the sale price?
items.e: Discount: 10% of $40 = $4. Sale price: $40 − $4 = $36. ($30 subtracts 10 dollars, not 10%; $44 adds the discount.)

items.q: What is the sale price of this rain jacket?
items.e: Discount: 25% of $60 = $60 ÷ 4 = $15. Sale price: $60 − $15 = $45. ($35 subtracts 25 dollars instead of 25%; $15 is the discount; $75 adds the discount.)

items.q: A pair of $80 hiking boots is 50% off. What is the sale price?
items.e: 50% off is half off. $80 ÷ 2 = $40. ($30 subtracts 50 dollars; $79.50 subtracts 50¢; $120 adds 50%.)

items.q: What is the sale price of this backpack?
items.e: This tag takes off dollars, not a percent. $50 − $15 = $35. ($42.50 takes off 15%; $65 adds the $15.)

items.q: A $35 board game is 20% off. What is the sale price?
items.e: Discount: 10% is $3.50, so 20% is $7. Sale price: $35 − $7 = $28. ($15 is 35 − 20; $7 is the discount; $42 adds the discount.)

items.q: An item is 30% off. Which calculation gives the sale price?
items.e: 30% off means you pay 100% − 30% = 70% of the price, so find 70% of the price. 30% of the price is only the discount.

items.q: What is the sale price of these skis?
items.e: Discount: 10% of $150 is $15, so 30% is $45. Sale price: $150 − $45 = $105. ($120 subtracts 30 dollars; $45 is the discount; $195 adds the discount.)

items.q: A $48 soccer ball is 25% off. What is the sale price?
items.e: Discount: 25% of $48 = $48 ÷ 4 = $12. Sale price: $48 − $12 = $36. ($23 is 48 − 25; $12 is the discount; $60 adds the discount.)

items.q: A $75 tent is 40% off. What is the sale price?
items.e: You pay 60%. 10% of $75 is $7.50, so 60% is 6 × $7.50 = $45. ($35 is 75 − 40; $30 is the discount; $105 adds the discount.)

items.q: A pair of $80 skates is on sale for $60. What percent is the discount?
items.e: Discount: $80 − $60 = $20. Compare it with the regular price: $20 out of $80 = 1/4 = 25%. (20% uses the dollars; 75% is the part you pay; 33% compares $20 with the sale price, $60.)

items.q: A $90 jacket can be bought at 20% off or with a $20-off coupon. Which deal saves more?
items.e: 20% of $90 = $18 off. The coupon is $20 off. $20 − $18 = $2, so the $20-off coupon saves $2 more. (“They save the same” mixes up 20% and $20; $18 is the 20% discount, not the difference.)

items.q: A $32 T-shirt is on clearance for 75% off. What is the clearance price?
items.e: 25% of $32 is $8, so 75% off is $24 off. You pay 25%: $8. ($24 is the discount; $16 is only 50% off; $31.25 takes off 75¢, not 75%.)

items.q: A bookstore deal: buy one book, get the second one 50% off. Two books cost $24 each. How much do the two books cost?
items.e: First book: $24. Second book: 50% of $24 off, so $12. Total: $24 + $12 = $36. ($48 forgets the discount; $24 makes the second book free.)

items.q: A store has “buy 2, get 1 free” on juice packs that cost $4.50 each. Ji-woo takes 3 packs. What does she pay for each pack?
items.e: She pays for 2 packs: 2 × $4.50 = $9.00. That buys 3 packs: $9.00 ÷ 3 = $3.00 per pack. ($4.50 forgets the free pack; $1.50 divides one price by 3; $13.50 is 3 packs with no deal.)

items.q: Store A sells a hockey stick for $60 at 15% off. Store B sells the same stick for $56 at 10% off. Which is cheaper?
items.e: Store A: 15% of $60 is $9, so $60 − $9 = $51.00. Store B: 10% of $56 is $5.60, so $56 − $5.60 = $50.40. Store B is cheaper, at $50.40. ($45.00 and $46.00 subtract the percent numbers as dollars.)

items.q: Arjun has $50. A $64 hoodie is 25% off. How much money does he have left after buying it?
items.e: Sale price: 25% of $64 is $16, so $64 − $16 = $48. Left: $50 − $48 = $2. ($16 is the discount; $11 uses $64 − 25 = $39; $34 subtracts only the discount from $50.)

items.q: A bike helmet is 20% off. The sale price is $40. What was the regular price?
items.e: The sale price is 80% of the regular price. 80% is $40, so 10% is $5 and 100% is $50. Check: 20% of $50 is $10 and $50 − $10 = $40. ($48 adds 20% of $40 instead; $60 adds 20 dollars; $32 takes 20% off again.)

items.q: A store gives $10 off when you spend $50 or more. Hana’s items cost $46. If she adds a $5 pair of socks, what happens?
items.e: With the socks: $46 + $5 = $51, which is $50 or more, so $10 comes off: $51 − $10 = $41. She pays $41, $5 less than $46, and gets the socks too.

items.q: A 2 kg bag of oats costs $9.00 and is 20% off. A 1 kg bag costs $3.80 and is not on sale. Which is the better buy?
c: The 1 kg bag, because it costs less
The 2 kg bag, by 20¢ per kg
The 1 kg bag, by 20¢ per kg
They cost the same per kg
items.e: Sale price of the 2 kg bag: 20% of $9.00 is $1.80, so $7.20. Per kg: $7.20 ÷ 2 = $3.60. 1 kg bag: $3.80 per kg. The 2 kg bag is better by 20¢ per kg. (Comparing totals, $3.80 and $7.20, is the mistake.)

items.q: Sofia wants headphones that cost $84. She saves $12 each week. How many weeks will it take?
items.e: Divide the goal by the savings each week: $84 ÷ $12 = 7 weeks. Check: 7 × $12 = $84. (72 comes from $84 − $12; 96 from $84 + $12.)

items.q: Nadia wants a video game that costs $90. She saves $12 each week. How many weeks until she has enough?
items.e: $90 ÷ $12 = 7.5. After 7 weeks she has 7 × $12 = $84, which is not enough. After 8 weeks she has $96. So it takes 8 weeks: round up. (78 comes from $90 − $12.)

items.q: Ryan has $35 saved. He wants a bike helmet that costs $110 and saves $15 each week. How many more weeks until he can buy it?
items.e: He still needs $110 − $35 = $75. $75 ÷ $15 = 5 weeks. (8 weeks forgets the $35 already saved; 10 weeks adds it; 3 weeks divides the $35 saved.)

items.q: Lucas wants to save $168 for a summer camp that starts in 12 weeks. How much must he save each week?
items.e: Share the goal over the weeks: $168 ÷ 12 = $14 a week. Check: 12 × $14 = $168. ($156 subtracts and $180 adds instead of dividing; $1.40 puts the decimal point in the wrong place.)

items.q: Ethan is saving for a skateboard. What percent of the goal has he saved?
items.e: $72 out of $96 = 72/96 = 3/4 = 75%. (72% uses the dollars as the percent; 25% is the part still needed.)

items.q: Leah saves $8 a week. How many more weeks until she reaches the goal?
items.e: Still needed: $96 − $72 = $24. $24 ÷ $8 = 3 weeks. (12 weeks divides the whole goal; 9 weeks divides the $72 already saved; 24 is the dollars needed.)

items.q: Owen earns $13 an hour babysitting and works 4 hours. He saves 25% of the money. How much does he save?
items.e: Earned: 4 × $13 = $52. 25% is one quarter: $52 ÷ 4 = $13. ($52 is all the money earned; $39 is the 75% left; $25 uses the percent as dollars.)

items.q: A Grade 6 class sets a goal of raising $500 at the Terry Fox Run. So far they have raised $320. What percent of the goal is that?
items.e: 320/500 = 64/100 = 64%. (36% is the part still to raise; 32% divides by 10 instead of 5; 156% divides 500 by 320.)

items.q: A class of 26 students goes on a field trip to Grouse Mountain. The bus costs $468. How much is the bus for each student?
items.e: Share the cost equally: $468 ÷ 26 = $18. Check: 26 × $18 = $468. ($442 subtracts 26; $1.80 misplaces the decimal.)

items.q: At a bake sale, the class sells 84 cookies for $1.25 each. How much money do they raise?
items.e: 84 × $1.25 = 84 × $1 + 84 × $0.25 = $84 + $21 = $105. ($84 forgets the 25¢; $85.25 adds instead of multiplying; $10.50 puts the decimal point in the wrong place.)

items.q: Mei buys a snack for $3.67 and pays cash with a $5 bill. Canada has no pennies, so a cash total rounds to the nearest 5¢. How much change does she get?
items.e: $3.67 is 2¢ from $3.65 and 3¢ from $3.70, so the cash total is $3.65. Change: $5.00 − $3.65 = $1.35. ($1.33 forgets the rounding; $1.30 rounds up to $3.70 and $1.40 rounds down to $3.60, but $3.65 is the nearest 5¢.)

items.q: In the summer, Harjot picks cherries in the Okanagan for $16 an hour. He works 7.5 hours. How much does he earn?
items.e: $16 × 7.5 = $16 × 7 + $16 × 0.5 = $112 + $8 = $120. ($112 leaves out the half hour; $128 uses 8 hours; $23.50 adds instead of multiplying.)

items.q: Ava saves $6 every week for a whole year. How much does she save?
items.e: A year has 52 weeks. 52 × $6 = $312. ($72 uses 12, the number of months; $58 adds 52 + 6; $24 is only about one month.)

items.q: A soccer team holds a car wash in Surrey. They wash 48 cars at $8 each. Soap and sponges cost $36. How much money do they make?
items.e: Money in: 48 × $8 = $384. Take away the cost of supplies: $384 − $36 = $348. ($384 forgets the supplies; $420 adds them; $92 adds all the numbers.)

items.q: Zara wants a $240 bike before the summer holidays, which start in 16 weeks. She already has $64 saved. How much must she save each week?
items.e: Still needed: $240 − $64 = $176. $176 ÷ 16 = $11 a week. Check: 16 × $11 = $176. ($15 forgets the $64 saved; $19 adds the $64; $4 divides $64 by 16.)

items.q: Two friends run a lemonade stand. Lemons, sugar and cups cost $12. They sell 40 cups for 75¢ each. What is their profit?
items.e: Money in: 40 × $0.75 = $30. Profit = money in − costs: $30 − $12 = $18. ($30 forgets the costs; $42 adds them; $288 reads 75¢ as $7.50.)

items.q: New skates cost $120. They go on sale for 25% off. Emma saves $15 a week. How many fewer weeks must she save because of the sale?
items.e: Sale price: 25% of $120 is $30, so $90. $90 ÷ $15 = 6 weeks. Without the sale: $120 ÷ $15 = 8 weeks. 8 − 6 = 2 weeks fewer. (6 weeks is the time with the sale and 8 weeks without it; 14 weeks adds them.)

items.q: The class has $75 for a party. They buy 6 pizzas at $11.50 each. How much money is left?
items.e: Pizzas: 6 × $11.50 = $69. Left: $75 − $69 = $6. ($63.50 subtracts the price of only one pizza; $69 is the cost, not what is left; $9 forgets the 50¢ on each pizza.)

items.q: Olivia earns $20 a week, spends $8.50 a week on snacks and saves the rest. Her goal is $92 for a lacrosse stick. How many weeks will it take?
items.e: Saved each week: $20.00 − $8.50 = $11.50. $92 ÷ $11.50 = 8 weeks. Check: 8 × $11.50 = $92. (5 weeks divides by all $20; 11 weeks divides by the $8.50 spent; 4 weeks also forgets to round up.)

items.q: Simran wants an $80 jacket. Next week it will be 15% off. She has $20 and saves $12 a week. How many weeks of saving until she can buy it at the sale price?
items.e: Sale price: 15% of $80 is $12, so $68. Still needed: $68 − $20 = $48. $48 ÷ $12 = 4 weeks. (5 weeks forgets the sale; 6 weeks forgets the $20; 7 weeks forgets both.)
